For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify it.
ground_truth_explanation:
Stipulated in the Austrian Framework for Open Government Platforms and the White Paper of the Cooperation OGD Austria, referring to the Open Principles and the Creative Commons Licence CC-BY 4.0. (https://www.data.gv.at/anleitung)

response to reviewers:
In Austria, the definition of open data reuse is stipulated in the Austrian Framework for Open Government Platforms and the White Paper of the Cooperation OGD Austria. It refers to the Open Principles and the Creative Commons Licence CC-BY 4.0. Specifically, open data reuse is defined as the use of data that is freely available to everyone to use, modify, and share for any purpose—subject to the terms specified under the Creative Commons Licence CC-BY 4.0. (Source: data.gv.at)

question:
Do you have a definition of open data reuse in your country?
 
For Explanation:
* If yes, please specify it.
ground_truth_explanation:
In France, according to a broad definition that is commonly accepted, « reuse » refers to the use of public data by third parties for purposes other than the public service mission for which the data was produced or received (this definition has been recalled in the legal guide provided by the French open data team : https://guides.data.gouv.fr/guides-open-data/guide-juridique/reutilisateurs-de-donnees/respecter-les-conditions-de-reutilisation). This definition directly stems from the Code of Relations between the Public and the Administration : « Public information contained in documents communicated or published by the administrations mentioned in the first paragraph of documents communicated or published by the administrations mentioned in the first paragraph of article L.300-2 may be used by any person who wishes to do so for purposes other than those of the public service mission for which the documents were produced or received. » (https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/article_lc/LEGIARTI000033219044)

This definition is similar to the PSI Directive definition : « Public sector bodies collect, produce, reproduce and disseminate documents in order to fulfill their public service mission. The use of these documents for other purposes constitutes reuse ».

The complexity and the need to clarify the definition of reuse has been emphasised in the literature, particularly with respect to research data, a key issue being the distinction between use and reuse. Besides that definition, more restrictive approaches have also emerged : some consider that only perennial uses of data are reuses while others consider any use of data as reuse. In our day to day operations, any exploitation of data in order to obtain information is considered as reuse, whether this exploitation is freely accessible or not : following that definition, a use of private data or a data journalist’s work to prepare for an investigation will be considered as reuse.

ground_truth_explanation:
Yes, there is an open data law at federal level. In July 2017, Section 12a of the E-Government Act (EGovG) entered into force (First Open Data Act), which for the first time created a legal basis for the mandatory provision of open administrative data by federal authorities. The Second Open Data Act, which entered into force in July 2021, further adapted the content of the existing obligations under Section 12a of the EGovG and extended them to the entire federal administration.

The Data Use Act (DNG) which also entered into force on 23 July 2021 aims to modernise and replace the Information Re-Use Act (IWG). In order to improve the usability of data, open data will need to be used in machine-readable formats. In addition, the DNG stimulates open data initiatives beyond the boundaries of the federal administration and establishes the principle of ‘open by default’ also for the use of data by the Länder, municipalities and public undertakings in the areas of water, transport and energy supply. The DNG also transposes EU Directive 2019/1024 (Open Data and Public Sector Information-Directive), which was recast in 2019.

question:
Does the national strategy/policy include an action plan with measures to be implemented in the open data field?

For Explanation:
If yes, please briefly describe the main measures described by the action plan.
ground_truth_explanation:
The Open Data Act obliges the Federal Government to report regularly to the German Parliament (Bundestag) every two years on the progress made in implementing open data (Section 12a (11) of the EGovG), see: http://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/egovg/__12a.html. The last progress report has been published in February 2025:
https://dserver.bundestag.de/btd/20/150/2015020.pdf?bcsi_scan_6dfde44891f17c0f=LMKxRqvgz5vof44GXw5bzhWuK7gRAAAAXhMgHw==&bcsi_scan_filename=2015020.pdf

The Open Data Strategy provides for various implementation measures, such as initiatives, projects and digital solutions. Parallel to this, a monitoring process has started in 2022 to document the implementation of individual measures, including through milestones and regular status reports.
https://www.bva.bund.de/DE/Services/Behoerden/Beratung/Beratungszentrum/OpenData/Monitoring/monitoring_node.html

Yes, Germany's national open data strategy includes a comprehensive action plan with concrete measures. The Open Data Strategy is a five-year plan that spans three main areas: enhancing data provision and building sustainable data infrastructure; promoting innovative, socially beneficial, and responsible data use; and fostering data competencies along with a cultural shift towards increased data quality and usability across federal administration. The strategy contains 68 specific implementation measures distributed among various federal ministries and agencies. To support execution, all federal authorities are mandated by the Second Open Data Act to appoint Open Data Coordinators responsible for standards and processes of data provision. Coordination networks and regular meetings among these coordinators facilitate cross-agency collaboration. Furthermore, the implementation progress is monitored and published online, underscoring a structured roadmap and operational delivery framework linked directly to the open data policy.
